title: The US and India Are in 'Sensitive' Talks Over Who Gets Access to the World's Most Powerful AI
excerpt: Washington says it's taking a 'gradual, measured approach' to releasing Anthropic's frontier models to India. New Delhi says it needs guarantees that access won't be yanked away.
body:
The United States and India are locked in what a senior American official calls "very sensitive national security discussions" about access to the world's most powerful artificial intelligence models — and the outcome will shape whether Indian companies, government agencies, and critical infrastructure can rely on American AI technology without fear of sudden cutoffs.

Jacob Helberg, the U.S. Under Secretary of State for Economic Growth, Energy, and the Environment, confirmed in an interview with ANI that Washington is pursuing a "gradual, measured approach" to releasing advanced AI models, including Anthropic's newest systems, to India and other trusted partners.

"Both sides really understand each other's perspectives," Helberg said. "Our intention is very much to continue a gradual measured approach to how we release Anthropic's models in a way that is safe, both for ourselves but also for our Indian counterparts."

The discussions come after the U.S. Commerce Department issued an export control directive in June requiring Anthropic to restrict foreign nationals from using its newly launched models, Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5. The directive sent a chill through India's AI ecosystem, where government agencies and enterprises have been building applications on top of American foundation models.

India's Core Fear: Abrupt Cutoffs

Speaking on the sidelines of the 2nd Pax Silica Summit in Washington, S. Krishnan, Secretary of India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, laid out New Delhi's central concern. "We sought an understanding of how exactly the US is looking at this particular aspect," he said. "If it is something which is to be used and made available, we can't have abrupt cutoffs."

Krishnan said India was given assurances. "We were given an understanding of how the US looks at this particular issue and how, going forward, they will ensure that for trusted partners, access will not be an issue."

The fear is not hypothetical. An abrupt withdrawal of access to foundational AI models could affect India's power grid management systems, digital public infrastructure, and enterprise platforms that have begun integrating advanced AI capabilities. Geopolitical shifts, commercial decisions by technology providers, or new export regulations could all trigger such disruptions.

A Closed-Door Roundtable

The AI discussions were part of a broader closed-door roundtable organised by the Indian Embassy in Washington alongside the U.S.-India Strategic Partnership Forum (USISPF) and the Silverado Policy Accelerator. Ambassador Vinay Mohan Kwatra, MeitY Secretary Krishnan, and U.S. Deputy Under Secretary of Commerce Bill Guidera addressed Indian and American companies working across semiconductors, critical minerals, and AI.

The discussions focused on "addressing shared barriers for investment, creating durable demand signals, and opportunities for AI collaboration at various levels, including frontier and application," the embassy said.

Additional Secretary (Americas) Nagaraj Naidu from the Ministry of External Affairs, USISPF President Mukesh Aghi, and Deputy Assistant Secretary Christopher Saldana from the U.S. Department of Energy also participated.

The Pax Silica Framework

These talks build on India's formal entry into Pax Silica, a U.S.-led coalition of trusted nations committed to securing the full AI supply chain — from critical mineral extraction and semiconductor fabrication to frontier model deployment. India became the 10th nation to join the alliance earlier this year, alongside Australia, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, the UK, Israel, the UAE, Greece, and Qatar.

Helberg has described the coalition as "not merely an agreement on paper, but a roadmap for a shared future." At the signing ceremony, IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said India's engineers are already "designing the world's most advanced two-nanometer chips" and that the semiconductor industry will need around one million new skilled professionals.

What This Means for the Tech Industry

For India's technology sector — and for the estimated 300,000 Indians working in Silicon Valley and the broader U.S. tech ecosystem — these discussions carry weight beyond geopolitics. If India secures reliable, long-term access to frontier AI models, it strengthens the case for building AI-driven products and services in India for global markets. If access remains uncertain, Indian enterprises may accelerate investment in homegrown foundation models as a hedge.

The broader subtext is the evolving nature of the U.S.-India technology partnership. What began as a relationship defined by IT outsourcing and visa-dependent labour mobility is transforming into a partnership over critical technologies: AI, semiconductors, quantum computing, and the minerals that power them all.

The next milestone is expected when Prime Minister Modi visits Washington for a state visit, where several deliverables related to frontier AI access and technology cooperation are expected to be finalised.
